content: The formulation of recommendations, including the identification of research priorities, was conducted systematically. Planning for dissemination, implementation, equity, ethical considerations, and impact evaluation, as well as updating the guideline, were integral components of the process. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was employed to prepare evidence profiles for preselected topics, utilizing up-to-date systematic reviews. The guideline development group was composed of content experts, methodologists, and representatives of potential stakeholders and beneficiaries. One group participated in a meeting in Geneva, Switzerland, from February 22–25, 2010, to define the scope of the guideline. A second group convened in Cancun, Mexico, from November 3–6, 2014, to discuss the evidence and finalize the recommendations. External experts served as resource persons, assisting the group by presenting evidence and identifying research priorities. Seven technical experts were invited to peer-review the draft guideline. Eight systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the effects of fortifying staple foods, including maize flour and cornmeal, with vitamins and minerals on critical nutritionand health-related outcomes. These reviews demonstrated positive effects on nutritional status when fortified foods were used to address dietary micronutrient deficiencies compared to no intervention. However, evidence on the effects of fortified maize flour for specific nutrients such as vitamin A, zinc, vitamin D, and calcium was limited or confounded by simultaneous fortification of multiple food items, as seen in programs in Brazil and Venezuela. Fortification of maize flour with folic acid or iron showed positive health outcomes in the general population. Iron fortification, when combined with other micronutrients, reduced the risk of iron deficiency but did not significantly impact anemia in children. The addition of folic acid to wheat and maize flour in the United States and other countries significantly improved folate intake, blood folate concentrations, and reduced the prevalence of neural tube defects. For some subpopulations, fortifying nixtamalized maize flour with folic acid could potentially reduce disparities in folate intake, particularly among Latino women in the U.S. compared to white populations. The overall quality of direct evidence for fortifying maize flour and cornmeal with vitamins and minerals as a strategy to improve population health was rated as very low for critical outcomes such as iron status, iron deficiency anemia, and folate status. There was no direct evidence for outcomes like neural tube defects, congenital anomalies, zinc status, growth, or adverse effects in children, including gastrointestinal symptoms. The guideline emphasizes that while direct evidence for maize flour or cornmeal fortification is limited, evidence from other staple food fortification programs demonstrates significant reductions in deficiency-related outcomes and improvements in population health. Countries are encouraged to integrate maize flour and cornmeal fortification into national programs to prevent and control micronutrient deficiencies. The choice and concentration of nutrients for fortification should consider the nutritional needs and dietary gaps of target populations, usual consumption levels, sensory and physical effects of fortificants, and other ongoing nutrition interventions. Restoration of B-complex vitamins, such as niacin, riboflavin, and thiamine, removed during milling and degerming, should remain a standard practice in maize flour fortification, particularly for non-nixtamalized maize flour. This approach has contributed to the near-elimination of beriberi and pellagra in many countries. Countries that fortify maize flour often also fortify wheat flour. A combined fortification strategy using multiple food vehicles may effectively reach all population segments. In such cases, selecting a combined fortification formula applicable to both types of flour may be appropriate. The choice of iron compound for fortification involves balancing cost, bioavailability, micronutrient interactions, and sensory acceptance. Nixtamalized flour, commonly used in the Americas, is more reactive to ferrous compounds, and the use of electrolytic iron appears ineffective for its fortification. Adding vitamin C and removing phytates in maize flour and cornmeal could enhance iron bioavailability. Food fortification should adhere to national standards, with quality-assurance and quality-control systems in place to ensure high-quality implementation. Continuous monitoring and evaluation of fortification programs are essential to assess their efficacy and effectiveness across all age groups. Research priorities include determining appropriate nutrient levels and combinations, understanding micronutrient interactions, and evaluating the impact of maize use for biofuel production on food security and fortification program sustainability. This guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations for fortifying maize flour and cornmeal with micronutrients to address dietary deficiencies and improve population health. It aims to support Member States in achieving Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to ending hunger, improving nutrition, and promoting health and well-being. The recommendations are intended for policymakers, technical experts, and program staff involved in designing and implementing nutrition interventions, particularly food fortification programs.
